## Concepts and intuitions {.unnumbered} -->

::: {style="margin-top: 1em; font-size: 125%; font-weight: 1000; text-align: center;"}
Ity kosa azoko e! Sa?
:::


Among all concepts, the mean is probably the one that everyone is familiar with a sight of relief. Everyone is capable of calculating the mean of a sequence: "the somme des nombres divisée par le nombre d'effectif". Yet, when one presents the equation for calculating the mean (see formal below @eq-mean_A and @eq-mean_B), it could appear inaccessible. Maybe with @sec-sum,  it is no longer the case.

There are three equivalent formulas to calculate the mean.
The part above is level one when calculating the mean. The other example is related to calculating the mean when there are coefficient involved: you multiply the grade with the coefficient, sum the whole thing, and then divide the sum of all the coefficients.

The third and final formula is to multiply each value by its frequency of occurence and then add these products. Or in the example of grade, instead of multiplying by the coefficient, you multiply by the coefficient divided by the sum of all coefficient. That final formulation allows us to calculate the mean using the distribution @sec-distribution, that is the weight is simply the frequency. Whereas the first approach is the simplest to implement, the last one is a generalized version that could be extended later.

The mean is probably the most used metric to summarize a data. However, boiling a sequence to single number means that many information (potentially valuable) are lost. If one student had 10/20 and 10/20 in two test, and another student has 5/20 and 15/20. One has to be careful to cimpare only the mean of the students. Finally, the most used one does not mean it is the best nor the only choice.


## Formal {.unnumbered}

The mean for data is applied stat

<!-- $$
    \bar{X} = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} X_i
$${#eq-mean-1} -->
$$
   \bar{X} =  \mu = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} x_i
$${#eq-mean_A}

The second version is that same $x_i$ repeats $n_i$ times, and $\sum n_i  = n$ the equation for the mean is

$$
    \mu =  \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i} n_i \, x_i
$${#eq-mean_B}

The third version is instead of multiplying by $n_i$ we multiply by $p_i = \frac{n_i}{n}$

$$
    \mu =  \sum_{i} p_i \, x_i
$${#eq-mean_C}

## Examples {.unnumbered}
Assume the grade is {5, 7, 10, 10, 12, 14}.

V1: $\frac{5 + 7 + 10 + 10 + 12 + 14}{6}$
V2: $\frac{5 + 7 + 2 \times 10 + 12 + 14}{6}$
V3: $\frac{1}{6} \times 5 + \frac{1}{6} \times 7 + \frac{2}{6} \times 10 + \frac{1}{6} \times 12 + \frac{1}{6} \times 14}$

V3 is just V2 where we divided the coefficient by the common denominator.


## Tips and warnings {.unnumbered}
- Mean is a metric that calculate captures the central tendency of the data.
- Mean only works with a quantitative variable so that the $n_i \times x_i$ makes sense.
- Semantic: mean and average are synonymous, expectation or expected value E[X] of firest order moment but the latter is used but mostly in the theoretical world.
- Mean can be misleading if there are exceeding large number. For instance intepreting the mean of 1, 1, 1, 1, 10 million is probably meaningless.
- Imagine we travel from Fianarantsoa to Ambalavao, on way travel, convince yourself that the taking the average of the speed does not give you the average speed.
- In this entire section, we mostly talked about arithmetic mean. There are different ways of calculating the mean, namely the geometric and the harmonic mean. For instance, in the speed example above calculating the harmonic mean will give the correct/intepreatble mean.

When analyzing the concept of "the mean" in statistics, textbooks bifurcate the definition based on the split you noted: applied statistics (which deals with observed data from a sample) and theoretical statistics (which deals with the underlying probability distributions and expected values of a population).
Here are the rigorous definitions for both, complete with textbook sources and raw LaTeX formatting.

1. Applied Statistics: The Sample Mean
In applied statistics, the mean is an empirical statistic computed directly from an observed sample of data. It serves as the primary measure of central tendency for a dataset.

Textbook Source
Book: Statistical Inference (2nd Edition, 2002)
Authors: George Casella and Roger L. Berger
Publisher: Duxbury / Thomson Learning

The Definition
In Chapter 5 ("Properties of a Random Sample"), Casella and Berger define the sample mean as a functional mapping of a finite sequence of observations:
Definition 5.2.2: "Let X1,…,Xn be a random sample of size n from a population. The sample mean is the statistic defined by

$\bar{X} = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} X_i$

1. Theoretical Statistics: The Population Mean (Expected Value)
In statistical theory, the mean of a variable is not calculated from data points. Instead, it is defined as the mathematical expected value (E[X] or μ) of its probability distribution. This represents the long-run average value if an experiment were repeated infinitely.

Textbook Source
Book: Introduction to Mathematical Statistics (8th Edition, 2019)
Authors: Robert V. Hogg, Joseph W. McKean, and Allen T. Craig
Publisher: Pearson

The Definition
In Chapter 1 ("Probability and Distributions"), the authors define the theoretical mean for both discrete and continuous domains under the umbrella of Mathematical Expectation.
A. The Discrete Theoretical Mean
"Let X be a discrete random variable with a probability mass function (pmf) p(x) and space D. If the sum converges absolutely, the mean (or expected value) of X, denoted by μ or E[X], is defined by
$\mu = \mathbb{E}[X] = \sum_{x \in \mathcal{D}} x \cdot p(x)$
"
B. The Continuous Theoretical Mean
"Let X be a continuous random variable with a probability density function (pdf) f(x). If the integral converges absolutely, the mean (or expected value) of X is defined by
$\mu = \mathbb{E}[X] = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} x \cdot f(x) \, dx$
"

Summary: How Theory and Application Intersect
The relationship between applied mean and theoretical mean is the foundation of inference.
As defined by the Weak/Strong Law of Large Numbers (LLN) in theory textbooks, if you repeatedly draw a larger and larger sample size (n→∞) from an underlying population distribution, your applied sample mean (bar(X)) is guaranteed to mathematically converge to the theoretical population mean (μ):

$\lim_{n \to \infty} P(|\bar{X}_n - \mu| < \varepsilon) = 1 \quad \text{for any } \varepsilon > 0$
